extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; critics evaluating Restoration drama and moral representation in literature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging moral representation, realism, and authorial responsibility in Restoration (late 17th-century) comedy; includes how to treat 'conventional worlds' versus realistic settings and the historical causes affecting dramatic morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional-world defence (Charles Lamb's doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatists of the latter part of the seventeenth century are not, according to him, to be tried by the standard of morality which exists, and ought to exist in real life. Their world is a conventional world... 'They belong to the regions of pure comedy, where no cold moral reigns. When we are among them we are among a chaotic people. We are not to judge them by our usages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defence that a playwright who constructs a fully conventional/utopian comic world should not be judged by ordinary moral standards. Examples Lamb uses implicitly: heroes/heroines not belonging to England/Christendom but to 'an Utopia of gallantry' or 'Fairyland.' Macaulay presents this as an arguable position but labels it 'altogether sophistical' when applied to plays that mimic real life. Use this criterion only when the fictional world is demonstrably alien to real-world social institutions and dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different kinds of conventional worlds (harmless vs dangerous)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible for a writer to create a conventional world in which things forbidden by the Decalogue and the Statute Book shall be lawful, and yet that the exhibition may be harmless, or even edifying... The conventional worlds of Fenelon and Mr. Southey are unobjectionable... the morality of these conventional worlds differs from the morality of the real world only in points where there is no danger that the real world will ever go wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral content, distinguish between conventional worlds that are radically unlike ours (e.g., Telemachus, Dialogues of the Dead, Thalaba) — where displayed virtues/vices pose no realistic contagion — and those that closely resemble contemporary society. Examine whether the fictional moral code could plausibly influence or be adopted by real readers/audiences; if not, the depiction is less objectionable. Examples and anti-patterns: Fenelon/Southey (harmless) vs. Wycherley/Congreve (dangerous because realistic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism of setting determines moral accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Here the garb, the manners, the topics of conversation are those of the real town and of the passing day... The scene is laid in some place which is as well known to the audience as their own houses... And the immorality is of a sort which never can be out of date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a play's world is populated with the everyday trappings, institutions, and recognizably contemporary social types (parks, courts, lawyers, peers, inns of court), it should be judged by real-world moral standards because its examples can influence or mirror actual behaviour. Anti-pattern: treating a realistic depiction as if it belonged to a harmless 'Utopia' to excuse immorality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as imitation must engage moral rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If comedy be an imitation, under whatever conventions, of real life, how is it possible that it can have no reference to the great rule which directs life, and to feelings which are called forth by every incident of life?... Pure comedy into which no moral enters [is] less consonant with sound criticism than pure landscape-painting into which no light or shade enters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comedies on their moral engagement: good comedic imitation should include moral 'light and shade' — references to the norms that guide life. A work that entirely avoids moral reference is defective as imitation. Use analogies (portrait/landscape painting lacking expression/light) to test whether the moral dimension is present or intentionally omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial responsibility in making immoral characters attractive
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a man of genius who constantly and systematically endeavours to make this sort of character attractive, by uniting it with beauty, grace, dignity, spirit, a high social position, popularity, literature, wit, taste, knowledge of the world, brilliant success in every undertaking, does or does not make an ill use of his powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an author glamorizes an immoral code by endowing its practitioners with admirable qualities (beauty, wit, status). If the work consistently makes vice alluring and admirable without corrective moral framing, the author is culpable of misusing artistic power. Example anti-pattern: treating libertine rakes as objects of aspiration without irony or consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation corresponds to real social types (not 'chaotic people')
rubrics_metrics.description: The morality of the Country Wife and the Old Bachelor is the morality... of low town-rakes, and of those ladies whom the newspapers call 'dashing Cyprians.'... We need not go to Utopia or Fairyland to find them. They are near at hand. Every night some of them cheat at the hells in the Quadrant, and others pace the Piazza in Covent Garden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the characters and moral codes depicted correspond to actual social groups and behaviours of the author's society. If so, the play is doing social reportage/representation and must be read as engaging with real social consequences rather than mere fantasy. Evidence: local details, recognizable vices (cheating, debauchery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical placement: whether sound morality is insulted and unsound morality celebrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Morality constantly enters into that world, a sound morality, and an unsound morality; the sound morality to be insulted, derided, associated with everything mean and hateful; the unsound morality to be set off to every advantage, and inculcated by all methods, direct and indirect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the work's stance is to mock/reduce sound moral positions while elevating unsound ones. Identify techniques used (association with ugliness/hypocrisy for the former; glamour/endorsement for the latter). This is distinct from neutral depiction: it is active endorsement/derision and bears on authorial intent and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of localising detail to create apparent realism
rubrics_metrics.description: A hundred little touches are employed to make the fictitious world appear like the actual world. And the immorality is of a sort which never can be out of date,... The lawyer bustles about with his bag, between the Common Pleas and the Exchequer. The Peer calls for his carriage to go to the House of Lords on a private bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a play's moral effect, note the micro-details that anchor it in a recognisable present (specific places, professions, customs). Such detail increases the play's potential to influence real audiences and thus increases the responsibility of representation. Anti-pattern: claiming 'conventionality' while using recognisable contemporaneous detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and social context must inform moral critique
rubrics_metrics.description: This great depravation of the national taste was the effect of the prevalence of Puritanism under the Commonwealth... The Restoration crushed for a time the Puritan party, and placed supreme power in the hands of a libertine. The political counter-revolution assisted the moral counter-revolution, and was in turn assisted by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should situate works in their socio-historical context: political repression, religious fashion, or recent upheavals shape the tone and tolerances of drama. Evaluate whether immorality is a reactive social phenomenon (a backlash against Puritanism, court fashions), and whether contemporary audiences would have interpreted works as social commentary, relief, or endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and enforced sanctity produce hypocrisy and backlash (limits of state moral enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To punish public outrages on morals and religion is unquestionably within the competence of rulers. But when a government, not content with requiring decency, requires sanctity, it oversteps the bounds which mark its proper functions... reward and punishment [are] altogether impotent for the purpose of touching the heart... The public discovers that the grave persons... are more utterly destitute of moral principle... And, as usual, it rushes to the extreme opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering both the creation and reception of immoral representation, account for the effects of governmental or institutional moral enforcement: heavy-handed moral law produces outward conformity, hypocrisy, and eventual licentious reaction. Use this principle to explain why periods of strict censorship are often followed by particularly licentious artistic movements; it is explanatory context rather than a stylistic guideline, but informs ethical evaluation of works.
